passage:
Wednesday, 11 p.m.
Helped Hemant with his quarterly report today. Two hours. He was drowning. Honestly, I only said yes because he sits with the regional manager at lunch and might mention my name. Added it to my list: Hemant owes me two now. I keep a note in my phone of who owes what. It works. People know I'm fair. I've never let anyone down on a trade. But at the team outing on Sunday, everyone was laughing about Nidhi's birthday surprise, and I realised no one had told me about it. I sat on the edge, sipping my cold drink. Fair dealing keeps things neat. I just wonder why the table felt so wide.
– Raghav

qa.q: How long did Raghav spend helping Hemant with the report?
qa.a: Two hours.

qa.q: What was Raghav thinking when he said yes to Hemant?
qa.a: Raghav felt hopeful that Hemant might mention Raghav's name to the regional manager, so the help was a kind of investment.

qa.q: What could Raghav try if he wanted closer relationships at work?
qa.a: Raghav could help someone once without adding it to the list, and join in team plans like birthday surprises, not just trades.

qa.q: How might Hemant see Raghav's help if he knew about the list?
qa.a: Hemant might feel the help was less warm than it seemed, and treat Raghav more as a trading partner than a friend.

grounding: An adult's diary shows helping a colleague only for future payoff and keeping a ledger of favours, which leaves relationships thin.

qa.q: What did Gurpreet want in return for covering Saturday?

qa.q: What does Nirmala's 'thanks I guess' suggest about how Nirmala feels?

qa.q: What could Gurpreet do differently to build trust with colleagues?
qa.a: Gurpreet could sometimes help without asking for extra, especially for family events, so colleagues feel cared for, not charged.

grounding: A chat shows an adult who helps a colleague only for a return and keeps a list of favours, leaving the relationship thin.

passage: At the cooperative bank branch in the market town, Hemant was known as the fairest clerk. If you covered his counter for an hour, he covered yours for an hour. If you brought him tea, he'd bring you tea next day. He kept a small notebook in his drawer: names, dates, favours. When Raghav, the new clerk, got stuck with a loan file and asked for help, Hemant thought, what's he done for me? He helped, but wrote it down. Months later, when Hemant's mother was in the district hospital, the others visited each other's families with food and flowers. No one came for his. Raghav sent a polite text. Hemant sat in the ward corridor, turning the notebook over in his hands.

qa.q: What did Hemant keep in his drawer?
qa.a: A small notebook with names, dates and favours.

qa.q: What might Hemant be feeling in the ward corridor?
qa.a: He may feel lonely and confused, wondering why no one came even though he always dealt fairly.

qa.q: What turning point might lead Hemant to change, and how?
qa.a: Sitting alone in the corridor with the notebook, Hemant could realise fair trades don't build closeness and start helping without keeping count.

qa.q: How might Raghav have felt about Hemant's help months earlier?
qa.a: Raghav probably felt helped but not cared for, which may be why he only sent a polite text later.

grounding: A clerk who keeps a ledger of favours finds that fair dealing left his work relationships thin when he needed support.

passage:
In the marketing office in Amman, Yara, twenty-six, stayed late to help Nkechi finish her slides for the director. Not because Nkechi was drowning, though she was. Because Nkechi ate lunch with the director twice a week.
On the bus home, Yara opened a note on her phone. Nkechi: owes me one, big. Under it were other entries: Omar covered my Friday, I owe him a coffee. Hana helped with Excel, returned. It was all very fair. She never took more than she gave.
A month later, Nkechi stopped at Yara's desk, eyes red. "My father's in hospital back home. I just needed to tell someone."
Yara said, "Oh no, I'm sorry," and then didn't know what else to say. She realised she knew nothing about Nkechi's father, or anyone's family, or what anyone here loved. Nkechi nodded and walked away.
That night Yara looked at her list for a long time.

qa.q: How often did Nkechi eat lunch with the director?
qa.a: Twice a week.

qa.q: What did Yara realise when Nkechi told her about her father?
qa.a: With dismay, she realised she knew nothing about Nkechi's life or anyone else's, because she had only ever kept track of favours.

qa.q: What might Yara choose to do differently after looking at her list?
qa.a: She could start getting to know colleagues as people, asking about their lives and helping sometimes without writing it down.

qa.q: How might Nkechi have felt when Yara had nothing more to say?
qa.a: Nkechi probably felt lonely and let down, having reached out in pain to someone who could only offer a polite sentence.

grounding: It shows an adult who helps a colleague for future gain and keeps a ledger of favours, dealing fairly but finding her work relationships thin.

passage:
At the IT company in Pune, Mridul, twenty-five, had a rule: help people who can help you back. So when Sumit, from the team that decided next quarter's project allocation, asked for help fixing a stubborn bug, Mridul stayed two hours. Later he added a line in the notebook in his drawer: Sumit, 2 hours, allocation.
He was scrupulously fair. Whenever someone helped him, he paid it back within a week, exactly. People called him reliable.
In October, at the team's lunch table, everyone was passing Sumit's phone around: photos of his newborn daughter. People asked her name, told stories about their own kids, laughed. Mridul realised he hadn't known Sumit's wife was pregnant. He hadn't known Priti from testing had a son, or that Kiran had just moved house.
He smiled and said, "Congratulations," and ate his biryani in silence. Back at his desk, he opened the notebook and couldn't find a single entry that told him who anyone was.

qa.q: What did Mridul write in the notebook after helping Sumit?
qa.a: Sumit, 2 hours, allocation.

qa.q: What was Mridul feeling as he ate his biryani in silence?
qa.a: He felt left out and uneasy, realising that everyone else knew each other's lives while he knew only who owed whom.

qa.q: What choice could Mridul make after that lunch?
qa.a: He could start asking colleagues about their lives and helping without tracking the payoff, so his fairness comes with real connection.

qa.q: How do Mridul's colleagues seem to see him?
qa.a: They see him as reliable and fair, but perhaps not as someone to share personal news with, since his help always seems to be a trade.

grounding: It shows an adult who helps colleagues only when it may pay off and keeps a ledger of favours, dealing fairly but ending up with thin relationships.
